coachingPoints: Use ONE hand with a high, soft release — floaters are not push shots from the chest.
The runner works best at about 3-4 meters from the rim — too close and it's a layup, too far and it's a jumper.
Keep the ball on one side of your body to shield it from the chasing defender.
Runner: keep running through the shot. Floater: stop your momentum slightly for balance.
Add the shot to your game gradually — start stationary floaters, then add the run.
commonMistakes: Shooting the floater flat — it needs a high arc to drop over a big's outstretched arm.
Releasing with two hands — kills the touch and the extension.
Jumping too high — floaters are about quick release, not elevation.
Using it against a set, flat-footed defender — just keep driving and lay it up.
description: The in-between shot for small guards: a one-handed floater or runner launched over retreating bigs.
gameSituations: Pick-and-roll when the big drops deep — the classic 'in-between' window is wide open.
Beating a help defender who is backpedaling — shoot before they can set their feet.
Drives where you can't get all the way to the rim but the midrange jumper would be too slow.

howTo.detail: Drive into the lane at speed. As you reach the free-throw-line area, pick up your dribble — you should be about 3 to 4 meters from the basket.
howTo.title: Attack the in-between zone

howTo.detail: Take your final steps under control. Runner: keep your legs moving through the shot. Floater: plant your last step to steady yourself.
howTo.title: Footwork: run or plant

howTo.detail: Lift the ball with one hand, keeping the off-hand on it only until release. The shooting hand stays under or behind the ball.
howTo.title: One-hand lift

howTo.detail: Release the ball high and soft, well above the defender's reach. Extend your arm fully and let the ball float — the wrist does the work, not the shoulder.
howTo.title: High, soft release

howTo.detail: Aim for the top of the backboard rectangle or just over the front of the rim. High arc is non-negotiable — a flat floater gets blocked.
howTo.title: Arc it over the big

title: Runner & Floater
whatIsIt: The runner and floater are one-handed, close-to-mid-range shots taken on the move — a guard's answer to shot blockers. A runner is released while still moving forward; a floater is released from a more settled, planted position. Both are launched high and soft, dropping over retreating big men.

These shots fill the 'dead zone' between a layup and a jumper. When a big defender drops back to protect the rim, attacking guards who can't finish over them need a shot that goes up before the big can recover — that's exactly what the runner and floater do.
whyItMatters: Every guard eventually faces a shot blocker they can't finish over and a drop-coverage big waiting at the rim. Without an in-between game, those drives die. The floater turns the area defenses concede — the 3-to-4-meter zone — into a scoring zone.
